newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegro might back Milosevic, but not amendments.
newsitem.headline: Montenegro might back Milosevic, but not amendments.

text.p: Montenegro was likely to back Slobodan Milosevic's candidacy for the president of Yugoslavia but will block any moves to amend the federal constitution, a senior Montenegrin official said on Monday.

"I expect resistance to constitutional changes from both the Main board of the ruling Democratic Party of Socialists (DPS) and the majority of Montenegrin opposition," Goran Rakocevic, Montenegrin culture minister told Reuters.

Serbian President Milosevic was officially nominated by his Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) last week to stand for the presidency of Yugoslavia when the five-year mandate of incumbent Zoran Lilic expires on June 25.
Serbia and its tiny ally Montenegro comprise the new Yugoslavia formed after the violent break-up of the former six-member Balkan federation in 1991.
Milosevic, the real power in Yugoslavia, is due to complete his second term as president of Serbia and cannot stand again.
But to maintain ultimate power over the police, army, purse and policy he must change the federal constitution and that can be done only in consensus with Montenegro.

SPS vice-president Milorad Vucelic said the amendments to the federal constitution were needed to enable Milosevic to be elected by direct ballot and would not affect equality between the two republics.

But Montenegrins fear that they would be drafted to give unresticted powers to Milosevic and that they, with less than half a million voters compared to seven million in Serbia, could never vote their candidate into office.
"I think that our answer will be a clear and non-ambiguous 'no' to constitutional changes which would in any way put Montenegro in an underdog role in Yugoslavia," Rakocevic said.
As for Milosevic's nomination, Rakocevic was more positive given the fact that the SPS and DPS are coalition partners in the federal parliament.
"Such a proposition might receive support, primarily since it has been presented by our coalition partner. The man is the president of SPS and after all, the president of Serbia."
However, Rakocevic, himself was against the idea.
"My personal opinion is that the policial concept represented by Slobodan Milosevic is an obsolete one.
"That concept predominantly brought our country into this position of non-communication with the world," he said.
Rakocevic objects that "Milosevic's policy does not honestly enough and quickly enough pursue economic and political reform and democratisation of the country."
Rakocevic belongs to a reformist DPS faction led by Montenegrin Prime Minister Milo Djukanovic, who is at odds with the hardline Montenegrin President Momir Bulatovic.

Djukanovic, a charismatic 35-year old pro-western politician who severely rebuked Milosevic in public for his isolationist stances, has survived Bulatovic's attempts to oust him and consolidated party resistance to Belgrade.

The DPS governing Main Board is due to meet on Wednesday to discuss Milosevic's nomination and the move for constitutional amendments but could also vote to dismiss Bulatovic, Montenegrin government sources said.

"This conflict (between Djukanovic and Bulatovic) is more important than any politics, above any political career. This is a conflict over a modern, democratic, prosperous Montenegro, and I hope that we would be the winners in the end," Rakocevic told Reuters.
